chapter: Joe Lyde stories and bandstand tales
title: Water-glass mutes, Lyde's Shakespeare habit and the old musician character
summary: Kid Thomas and others use glass mutes. Lyde read Shakespeare nightly; Crawford and Zanco say old New Orleans musicians were defined by personality, and Johnny Lane reads Shakespeare on the stand.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, Kid Thomas is about the best one with the water glass around time. Does he use that?
And Panama is his specialty on that. Uh, let's see. Now, Joe, what else did he do? He owned Tiger Ride, you know, they had that whole lot of Tiger chorus. Did you ever see that?
Uh, where he would, uh, roar or yell.
Yeah, well, he, but he'd pull, when it came to hold that Tiger, he'd pull up a Christmas horn and blow it. That was really great.

I tell you, anybody, anybody that did see Joe in action, to me, Joe was the typical old, old, old time jazz musician. He just didn't care. He just wanted to play music. And, uh, I don't know, I've always admired Joe. I like Joe. I like his style. I like the way, maybe I, I would never think of action. I would never think of acting the way Joe acted on a bandstand, you understand? But, I mean, you had to appreciate what he was doing. Everything he did was just part of the show, you know?

I guess his, his personality is like Jeff Salsa told me one time. Jeff is a guy who goes to school, what's he studying? Philosophy? Psychology. Psychology. And, uh, he figured out one time, from talking to, talking and listening to George Gaynor and Jim Robinson, or maybe George talk about Jim, or something about those guys, that, that the old New Orleans style musician wasn't just a style of playing.
It was the character too, I believe. It was an absolute personality. Yeah.
With the, uh, with the guy. I mean, you just didn't play your art or anything. You, you, if you were a musician, well, that's what you were, and you weren't anything else.

Uh, incidentally, uh, Joe, Joe was a great, uh, Shakespearean fan, you know? Joe read Shakespeare every night of his life, man. And, I think when he graduated from high school, his mother had given him a, uh, oh, I think comedy tragedy and something or else, you know, all about Shakespeare. And, uh, it got to be like a tonic with him. Uh, you might say a, a sleep inducer. He had to read a few lines of Shakespeare every night before he went to sleep, you know? And, I mean, it was things like that that made a character of Joe, you know?

Well, Johnny Lane is the same. He sits up on the stand. This is a guy from Chicago that studied under Jimmy Newman. He sits up on the stand. On the stand. He might have had it right the first time. But anyways, he sits on the stand and reads Shakespeare, you know, between numbers. And Joe's Boonies will be playing with him. And he'll say, well, the next number is dedicated to our boss. High psychiatry. You know?
